questions.stem: The Rubicon was significant in January 49 BCE because it was:
options: the frontier between Rome's province of Spain and independent Gaul
the border that Pompey's army had to cross to reach Macedonia
the boundary between Caesar's province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy
the river that separated Transalpine Gaul from the lands of the Germans
questions.explanation: A governor could command troops only inside his province, so leading an army over the Rubicon into Italy was an act of war against the state. The Rhine, not the Rubicon, divided Gaul from the Germans.

questions.stem: Before Caesar's conquests, Rome already held Transalpine Gaul, often called simply 'the Province'. This region lay:
options: in the Alps, between the Po valley and the upper reaches of the Danube
on the Atlantic coast of Aquitania, around the mouth of the Garonne
on the Mediterranean coast of southern France, between Italy and Spain
in the far north of Gaul, along the Channel coast facing Britain
questions.explanation: The Province (later Gallia Narbonensis) secured the land route between Italy and Spain. Caesar's conquest took in the rest of Gaul, from the Province to the Channel and the Rhine.

questions.stem: Caesar opens his Gallic War by describing Gaul as divided into three parts, inhabited by:
options: the Belgae, the Aquitani and the Celts, whom the Romans called Gauls
the Helvetii, the Suebi and the Britons, who shared one language
the Nervii, the Veneti and the Arverni, each ruled by a single king
the Germans, the Iberians and the Ligurians, settled along the coast
questions.explanation: Caesar names the Belgae in the north, the Aquitani in the south-west and the Celts or Gauls in between. The Helvetii and Arverni were Gallic peoples, while the Suebi were German.

questions.stem: How did the careers of Marius and Sulla shape the world in which Caesar rose?
options: They created the office of emperor, which Caesar then inherited from Sulla
They showed that a general with a loyal army could take power in Rome by force
They restored the Senate's control of the army so firmly that no general could rebel
They abolished the tribunate, so Caesar could only work through the Senate
questions.explanation: Sulla's marches on Rome and the Marian-Sullan civil wars set precedents of armies loyal to their commanders. Sulla limited the tribunes rather than abolishing them, and the office of emperor came later with Augustus.

questions.stem: As a young man Caesar was named flamen Dialis, the priest of Jupiter. Losing this office under Sulla may have helped his career because the flamen Dialis:
options: was bound by taboos, such as never seeing an army, that barred command
had to live outside Rome on Jupiter's temple estate in the hills of Latium
could hold the office only until his thirtieth birthday and then had to retire
had to give all his family's property to the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol
questions.explanation: The flamen Dialis was bound by many taboos, such as not riding a horse or seeing an army under arms, which would have shut Caesar out of command. Without the post, he was free to follow a normal military and political career.

questions.stem: Sulla ordered the young Caesar to divorce his wife Cornelia, daughter of Cinna. According to the ancient sources, Caesar:
options: fled to Spain and raised an army to fight Sulla alongside the Marians
refused, lost his priesthood and property, and hid until he was pardoned
obeyed at once and was rewarded with a command in Sulla's army in the east
divorced her but married Sulla's daughter, which made him Sulla's heir
questions.explanation: Suetonius and Plutarch say Caesar refused, was stripped of his priesthood and his wife's dowry, and hid until relatives and the Vestal Virgins won him a pardon. His refusal marked him out as linked to Marius and Cinna.

questions.stem: Early in his career Caesar travelled to Rhodes to study:
options: military tactics, in the school of the Rhodian navy
law, under the jurist Quintus Mucius Scaevola
rhetoric, under the teacher Apollonius Molon
philosophy, under the Stoic teacher Posidonius
questions.explanation: Suetonius and Plutarch say Caesar went to Rhodes to study oratory with Apollonius Molon, who also taught Cicero. Skill in speaking was essential for courts and assemblies in Rome.

questions.stem: Suetonius says that while serving in Asia as a young man, Caesar won the civic crown at the capture of Mytilene. This award was given for:
options: saving the life of a fellow citizen in battle
being the first man over the walls of a city
winning a naval battle against the pirates
commanding the army to a victory as consul
questions.explanation: The corona civica, of oak leaves, honoured a soldier who saved a citizen's life. It was a high honour for a young man and gave early military prestige.

questions.stem: Caesar's marriages were Cornelia (daughter of Cinna), Pompeia (granddaughter of Sulla) and Calpurnia (daughter of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul in 58 BCE). He also married his daughter Julia to Pompey in 59 BCE. What do these marriages best show?
options: Caesar avoided links with Sulla's family throughout his career
Caesar used marriage as a political tool to build alliances
Caesar always married into the family of Marius's supporters
Roman law required senators to marry the daughter of a consul
questions.explanation: Each match linked Caesar to useful families, and Julia's marriage bound Pompey to him during the Triumvirate. Marrying Pompeia, Sulla's granddaughter, shows he did not avoid Sulla's family when it suited him.

questions.stem: As governor of Further Spain in 61-60 BCE, Caesar campaigned against the Lusitanians. The main political benefit of this command was that it:
options: gave him the support of Cato and the optimates for his consulship
allowed him to bring his army into Rome to force his election
brought him wealth to ease his huge debts and a claim to a triumph
made him governor of Gaul for the next ten years without election
questions.explanation: The Spanish command let Caesar pay creditors and win military credit. He gave up his claim to a triumph so that he could stand for the consulship of 59 BCE, since a general waiting for a triumph had to stay outside the city.

questions.stem: Caesar's first campaign in Gaul, in 58 BCE, was against:
options: the Britons, who were sending help to the Gauls across the Channel
the Veneti, whose ships controlled the trade of the Atlantic coast
the migrating Helvetii, and then the German king Ariovistus
Vercingetorix and the Arverni, who had united the Gauls in a great revolt
questions.explanation: In 58 BCE Caesar turned back the Helvetii and then defeated Ariovistus. The Veneti were fought in 56 BCE, Britain was invaded in 55 and 54, and Vercingetorix's revolt came in 52.

questions.stem: In 56 BCE Caesar's fleet defeated the Veneti, whose tall sailing ships were hard to ram. According to Caesar, the Romans won by:
options: blockading the Veneti until they surrendered without a battle
hiring Greek ships from Massilia that were larger than the enemy's
using hooks on long poles to cut the rigging so the ships could not sail
setting fire to the enemy fleet with burning arrows while it lay in harbour
questions.explanation: Caesar says sharpened hooks on poles cut the halyards, bringing down the sails and leaving the ships helpless when the wind dropped. Roman marines could then board them one by one.

questions.stem: In 55 BCE Caesar built a timber bridge across the Rhine, crossed with his army, stayed briefly and then destroyed it. His main purpose was to:
options: escape the Senate's order recalling him to Rome to face prosecution
show the Germans the reach of Roman power and deter them from Gaul
conquer Germany as far as the Elbe and make it a new Roman province
find a land route to Britain that avoided crossing the Channel by sea
questions.explanation: Caesar says he wanted the Germans to fear Roman power, and building a bridge rather than using boats suited Roman dignity. He did not try to hold territory east of the Rhine.

questions.stem: In 52 BCE, before Alesia, Caesar failed to take the Gallic stronghold of:
options: Bibracte
Massilia
Gergovia
Avaricum
questions.explanation: Caesar was forced to withdraw from Gergovia, one of his few setbacks in Gaul. Earlier that year he captured Avaricum after a siege, and Bibracte was the site of his victory over the Helvetii in 58.

questions.stem: At Alesia Caesar built two lines of fortifications, one facing the town and one facing outwards. The outer line was needed because:
options: the Germans had promised to invade the Province while Caesar was busy
the Senate had ordered the town to be completely sealed off from trade
Vercingetorix planned to break out through a tunnel beyond the inner line
a large Gallic relief army was expected to attack the Romans from outside
questions.explanation: The inner works trapped Vercingetorix in Alesia, and the outer works protected the besiegers from the relief army summoned from across Gaul. When the relief failed, Vercingetorix surrendered.

questions.stem: Which combination best explains Caesar's success in the Gallic War?
options: Speed of movement, skilled engineering and the disunity of the Gallic peoples
A larger army than all the Gauls combined and help from the Germans throughout
Superior cavalry recruited in Italy and the use of war elephants in battle
Long sieges of every town, avoiding open battle until the Gauls starved
questions.explanation: Caesar moved fast, used engineering in sieges and bridges, and exploited rivalries among Gallic peoples, many of whom fought on his side. He was often outnumbered, and his cavalry was mostly Gallic and German.

questions.stem: Suetonius says Caesar addressed his soldiers not as 'soldiers' but as 'comrades' (commilitones). This practice was mainly intended to:
options: build a personal bond of loyalty between the general and his men
remind the soldiers that they had to obey the Senate before him
show that he regarded them as equal to senators in rank
persuade them to accept lower pay during long campaigns
questions.explanation: Caesar shared hardships, rewarded his men and spoke to them as fellow soldiers. Combined with generous pay and plunder, this tied the legions to him personally, which mattered in the Civil War.

questions.stem: In 47 BCE veterans of the Tenth Legion mutinied in Italy, demanding discharge and rewards. The sources say Caesar ended the mutiny by addressing them as 'citizens' (Quirites). This worked because:
options: it implied he had already discharged them, so they begged to serve again
Roman law forbade the punishment of any man addressed as a citizen by a consul
the word was a signal that he would pay their rewards in full that same day
it reminded them that they were Gauls who had been granted Roman citizenship
questions.explanation: By calling them civilians, Caesar treated them as no longer part of his army, and the shamed soldiers asked to keep serving. The story shows his skill in managing his men's pride and loyalty.

questions.stem: Suetonius reports that Caesar remained seated before the temple of Venus Genetrix when a group of senators came to present him with honours. Why did this cause offence?
options: It took place inside the senate house, where only consuls might sit
It insulted Venus, since only priests could sit before her temple
It treated the senators as inferiors, which seemed the behaviour of a king
It broke a law that the dictator had to stand when any magistrate spoke
questions.explanation: Rising to greet the Senate was expected courtesy, so staying seated suggested contempt and monarchy. Suetonius lists it among the acts that made Caesar hated.

questions.stem: Early in the Civil War, in 49 BCE, Caesar campaigned in Spain against Pompey's legates Afranius and Petreius. The campaign ended with:
options: the death of Pompey, who had come to Spain to command in person
a peace treaty under which Spain was divided between the two sides
their surrender near Ilerda after Caesar cut off their supplies
Caesar's defeat and retreat to Gaul, where he waited for reinforcements
questions.explanation: Caesar outmanoeuvred the Pompeian army near Ilerda and forced it to surrender, largely without a pitched battle. Pompey was then in Greece, and he died in Egypt in 48 BCE.

questions.stem: After his defeat at Pharsalus in 48 BCE, Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was:
options: welcomed by Cleopatra and given troops to continue the war
captured and handed over alive to Caesar, who pardoned him
made governor of Alexandria by the Egyptian royal court
killed on landing by men acting for the young king Ptolemy XIII
questions.explanation: Ptolemy XIII's advisers had Pompey killed, hoping to please Caesar. Caesar arrived soon after and became involved in the struggle between Ptolemy and Cleopatra.

questions.stem: The last major battle of Caesar's Civil War, fought against the sons of Pompey in Spain in 45 BCE, was:
options: Zela
Dyrrachium
Munda
Thapsus
questions.explanation: Munda in 45 BCE ended organised resistance. Thapsus (46) defeated the Pompeians in Africa, Zela (47) defeated Pharnaces of Pontus, and at Dyrrachium (48) Caesar was checked by Pompey.

questions.stem: Which statement about Mark Antony's role under Caesar is correct?
options: He was Caesar's master of horse and his fellow consul in 44 BCE
He led the conspiracy against Caesar and struck the first blow
He commanded Pompey's fleet before changing sides after Pharsalus
He was Caesar's adopted son and named as his heir in the will
questions.explanation: Antony was master of horse during Caesar's dictatorship and consul with him in 44 BCE. Caesar's will adopted Octavius, not Antony.

questions.stem: Marcus Brutus fought for Pompey at Pharsalus, was pardoned by Caesar and then promoted to the praetorship. Why does his part in the assassination matter to historians judging the conspirators' motives?
options: It proves the conspirators were all Pompeians who had never been pardoned
It shows that Caesar had planned to execute all his former enemies
It proves that Brutus wanted to become dictator in Caesar's place
It suggests some were moved by republican principle, not personal grievance
questions.explanation: Brutus owed Caesar his life and career, so his role is usually explained by his devotion to the Republic and his family's tradition of opposing kings. Other conspirators, though, had personal ambitions and grievances.

questions.stem: Which of these was a reform of Caesar's dictatorship?
options: Founding colonies abroad, such as Carthage and Corinth, for veterans
Cancelling all debts in Italy and seizing the estates of moneylenders
Abolishing the Senate and giving its powers to the tribal assembly
Ending the grain dole in Rome and giving the money to the army
questions.explanation: Caesar settled veterans and urban poor in colonies in the provinces, including refounded Carthage and Corinth. He eased debts but refused a general cancellation, and he reduced rather than ended the grain dole.

questions.stem: Caesar passed a law limiting how long a governor could hold a province. The most likely purpose was to:
options: reduce the number of provinces so that the army could be cut
give the Senate the right to choose governors by lot each month
stop other men building long commands and loyal armies as he had done
allow his own supporters to keep their provinces for life
questions.explanation: Caesar's own power rested on a long command in Gaul, so limiting tenure made it harder for a rival to repeat his path. It fits a pattern of measures to control the provinces and the army.

questions.stem: Caesar gave Roman citizenship to the people of Gaul north of the Po and enlarged the Senate with men from Italy and the provinces. Which judgement of these measures is most balanced?
options: They were purely acts of generosity with no political benefit to Caesar at all
They reversed the Social War settlement and took citizenship away from the Italians
They were opposed by Caesar's own soldiers, who refused to share citizenship
They widened the citizen body, but also filled the Senate with his supporters
questions.explanation: Extending citizenship and bringing new men into the Senate looked forward to the empire's later unity, yet the beneficiaries were often Caesar's clients. Both views appear in modern judgements.

questions.stem: Caesar was about to leave Rome for a long campaign against Parthia when he was killed. Why did this plan add urgency to the conspiracy?
options: The Senate had voted against the war, so Caesar planned to dissolve it
Caesar intended to move the capital to Parthia after his victory
Away with his army he would be out of reach, and might be named king
The campaign was to be led by Brutus, who did not want to leave Rome
questions.explanation: Ancient writers report a rumour that a prophecy said only a king could conquer Parthia, so a proposal to give him the title was expected. Absent for years with a great army, he would also be safe from attack.

questions.stem: Caesar was killed on the Ides of March, 44 BCE, at a meeting of the Senate held in:
options: the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, during a sacrifice
his own house on the Sacred Way, where the conspirators found him
the hall attached to Pompey's theatre, beside a statue of Pompey
the senate house in the Forum, rebuilt after the fire of 52 BCE
questions.explanation: The Senate met in the Curia of Pompey, part of his theatre complex, because the senate house in the Forum was being rebuilt. Caesar fell at the foot of Pompey's statue.

questions.stem: In the days after the murder, the Senate granted an amnesty to the conspirators but also confirmed Caesar's acts. Antony's funeral speech then turned the crowd, which burned Caesar's body in the Forum. What do these events best show?
options: The conspirators had removed Caesar but not his supporters or his popularity
The people of Rome rejoiced at the death of a tyrant and honoured the killers
The Republic was restored at once and ran smoothly for the next decade
Antony was a secret member of the conspiracy who now betrayed it
questions.explanation: Caesar's acts, veterans and popularity survived him, and the conspirators soon had to leave Rome. Civil war followed, ending in rule by one man again.

questions.stem: Suetonius says a comet appeared during games held in Caesar's honour in 44 BCE, and people believed it was his soul received into heaven. How was this used?
options: It led the Senate to cancel all the honours that had been voted to Caesar
It was taken as a sign that Antony should be made dictator for life
It supported Caesar's deification, which Octavian used to his advantage
It was used by Brutus and Cassius to prove that the gods approved the murder
questions.explanation: Caesar was officially deified as Divus Iulius in 42 BCE, and Octavian made great use of the title 'son of the divine'. The comet appeared on coins and statues of Caesar.

questions.stem: Sallust, a supporter of Caesar, compares Caesar and Cato in his Conspiracy of Catiline: Caesar admired for generosity and mercy, Cato for integrity and strictness. How should a historian use this passage?
options: As a hostile attack on Caesar written by one of his own assassins
As a stylised portrait by a partisan, showing how contemporaries saw Caesar
As an exact record of the speeches and votes in the Senate in 63 BCE
As proof that Cato and Caesar were close friends and political allies
questions.explanation: Sallust served under Caesar, and his paired portraits are literary and moral, written years later. They show valued qualities and contemporary images rather than a neutral record.

questions.stem: Lucan's epic poem on the Civil War, written under Nero, portrays Caesar as a destructive force. Its main limitation as evidence is that it:
options: was written by an officer who served under Caesar in Gaul
survives only in a few short quotations in later writers
was censored by Caesar himself before it was published
is a poem written a century later, hostile to one-man rule
questions.explanation: Lucan wrote in the reign of Nero, long after the events, with a republican and poetic purpose. It reveals later attitudes more than the facts of Caesar's career.
